claims.text: The starting alloy is DED-fabricated Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17.
The alloy is produced from blended 45–150 μm, 99.9%-pure elemental powders on a Ti6Al4V substrate.
The initial alloy has an average grain size of approximately 3.66 μm.
The initial alloy has a predominantly BCC A2 microstructure.
The initial alloy has a microhardness of approximately 720 HV.
Laser-assisted machining with controlled preheating produces a near-surface region with less machining-induced damage than conventional machining.
Approximately 800–930 °C is a near-surface softening regime for this alloy during laser-assisted machining.
A cutting depth of 0.3 mm can remove the laser-generated heat-affected layer while preserving the undamaged underlying microstructure.
Laser-assisted machining retains a coarser near-surface grain size of approximately 3.18 μm, compared with approximately 2.20 μm after conventional machining.
Laser-assisted machining reduces near-surface work hardening relative to conventional machining.
Laser preheating locally softens the alloy and thereby reduces cutting resistance.
Reduced cutting resistance suppresses machining-induced work hardening and severe grain refinement.
Removing the softened heat-affected layer leaves a more stable and less damaged machined surface.
The less damaged surface microstructure will provide higher elevated-temperature tensile strength than conventional machining.
The less damaged surface microstructure will provide a lower creep rate than conventional machining.
Conventionally machined specimens develop more pronounced grain refinement and work hardening than laser-assisted-machined specimens.
Conventionally machined specimens have a more extensive heat-affected zone than laser-assisted-machined specimens.
The predicted mechanical benefit applies during subsequent testing from 800 °C to approximately 1000 °C.
